questions.q:
Leadership is not a title one wears on a ceremonial day; it is the steady habit of making difficult decisions before the crowd can see the consequences. In any organisation, especially in the armed forces, disciplined leadership depends on clarity, trust, and emotional control. A leader who cannot remain calm under pressure will rarely inspire confidence in those who must act swiftly. Such a leader may issue orders, but cannot create a culture of obedience built on respect. The best commanders do not merely demand compliance; they explain the purpose behind a task, demonstrate fairness, and accept accountability when the outcome is poor. This is why professionalism is inseparable from leadership. When discipline exists, people know what is expected, where responsibility begins, and what standard must be maintained even in uncertain conditions. It is this consistency that turns routine service into trust. In a democracy, too, leadership must be transparent, because authority without accountability quickly becomes arbitrary. The challenge is not to dominate others but to guide them with judgment, restraint, and courage.

Which of the following best captures the central idea of the passage?
A. Leadership is successful only when authority is exercised without explanation.
B. Leadership is effective when it combines discipline, trust, and accountability with calm judgment.
C. Orders matter more than purpose in a disciplined organisation.
D. Professional behaviour is irrelevant to public confidence.
options: Leadership is effective when it combines discipline, trust, and accountability with calm judgment.
Leadership is successful only when authority is exercised without explanation.
Orders matter more than purpose in a disciplined organisation.
Professional behaviour is irrelevant to public confidence.

A. cynical and dismissive

The digital revolution has transformed the way citizens interact with government and with one another. E-governance, digital payments, and smart infrastructure have improved speed and convenience, yet they have also created new vulnerabilities. A system that is efficient but opaque can erode public trust, especially when citizens cannot understand how decisions are made or how their data is used. This is why technology must serve public accountability, not merely administrative convenience. Responsible innovation requires safeguards, clear rules, and informed public debate. When a city introduces intelligent traffic systems or digital land records, the gains are visible; the risks remain hidden until a breach, misuse, or exclusion occurs. Therefore, technology must be accompanied by ethical design and professional oversight. The purpose of modern administration is not simply to process numbers faster, but to protect rights, reduce exclusion, and build resilience in the face of uncertainty. Society gains most when technology expands opportunity without diminishing fairness or security.

A. Civic technology is only useful when it reduces the amount of paperwork.
B. Digital systems should be designed to improve efficiency while preserving trust, fairness, and privacy.
C. Public administration should avoid automation because it creates exclusion.
D. Government data systems are inherently secure and transparent.
options: Civic technology is only useful when it reduces the amount of paperwork.
Digital systems should be designed to improve efficiency while preserving trust, fairness, and privacy.
Public administration should avoid automation because it creates exclusion.
Government data systems are inherently secure and transparent.

Public trust in institutions is often built in small, ordinary ways rather than through dramatic announcements. A citizen who receives a clear response from a government office is more likely to accept the system as legitimate than one who is met with delay, confusion, or indifference. This is why effective administration depends not only on policy design but also on the quality of everyday interaction. When officers listen carefully, explain procedures patiently, and respond without bias, they create a culture of accountability. At the same time, institutions must remain open to feedback, because feedback is valuable only when it is used constructively. Without this discipline, even well-intentioned reforms may become rigid and unresponsive. Therefore, the real test of reform is not whether a rule is written clearly, but whether it is implemented consistently and understood by the people it is meant to serve. Good administration does not merely enforce order; it earns confidence and preserves public faith in the state.

questions.q:
Public trust in institutions is often built in small, ordinary ways rather than through dramatic announcements. A citizen who receives a clear response from a government office is more likely to accept the system as legitimate than one who is met with delay, confusion, or indifference. This is why effective administration depends not only on policy design but also on the quality of everyday interaction. When officers listen carefully, explain procedures patiently, and respond without bias, they create a culture of accountability. At the same time, institutions must remain open to feedback, because feedback is valuable only when it is used constructively. Without this discipline, even well-intentioned reforms may become rigid and unresponsive. Therefore, the real test of reform is not whether a rule is written clearly, but whether it is implemented consistently and understood by the people it is meant to serve. Good administration does not merely enforce order; it earns confidence and preserves public faith in the state.

9. The passage suggests that good administration
A. prioritises compliance over empathy
B. earns confidence by fairness and consistency
C. depends entirely on public applause
D. avoids accountability in difficult situations
options: earns confidence by fairness and consistency
